item.title: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation: Neuromodulation of the suprascapular nerve and brachial plexus for postoperative analgesia following ambulatory rotator cuff repair. A proof-of-concept study
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Brian M. Ilfeld; John J. Finneran; Rodney A. Gabriel; Jessica K. Sztain; James W. Abramson; Mark S. Wallace

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 7

Summary: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates **ultrasound-guided percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS)** of the suprascapular nerve and brachial plexus using small, temporary, implantable leads to provide postoperative analgesia after ambulatory rotator cuff repair, avoiding continuous local anesthetic infusions.[3] The key innovation is minimally invasive, *preoperative* ultrasound-guided lead placement enabling targeted neuromodulation of proximal shoulder nerves with an external stimulator, suggesting a scalable, modular interface concept that could inform **biorobotic systems for closed-loop motor–sensory neuromodulation**, peripherally implanted sensor–actuator networks, and non-opioid, wearable neuroprosthetic pain-control strategies.

DOI: 10.1136/rapm-2018-100121

item.title: Surface Electromyography vs Clinical Outcome Measures After Robot-assisted Gait Training in Patients with Spinal Cord Injury
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: **Elena Kaczmarek; Ewa Dziankowska-Zaborszczyk; Agnieszka Kujawa; Ewa Ptaszkowska; Wojciech Kiebzak; Marcin Kaczmarek**[7]

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 5

Summary: The paper demonstrates that **surface EMG (sEMG) can sensitively capture training‑induced changes in lower-limb muscle activation during Lokomat robot-assisted gait training in sub‑acute incomplete SCI**, and relates these changes to standard clinical outcome measures in 64 patients.[5][2] By quantitatively decoding muscle activation patterns rather than relying solely on functional scores, the work highlights sEMG as a **biomarker and control-relevant signal** that could inform adaptive control, patient-specific tuning, and objective performance monitoring in rehabilitation robots, advancing closed‑loop and biomimetic strategies in biorobotics.[5]

DOI: 10.26444/aaem/189609

item.title: New Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Electromyography-Driven Robot for Hand Rehabilitation After Stroke
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Xin Li; Xiaoling Hu; Xue Zhang; Wenbin Zhang; Jing Xu; Huaiqiang Sun; Mengnan Li; Yancheng You; Dingguo Zhang

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 5

Summary: The paper introduces an **AI-integrated EMG-driven hand exoskeleton** that uses surface EMG and a learning-based intention detection framework to decode user-specific finger flexion/extension intentions in real time and drive a multi-DOF rehabilitation robot accordingly. By tightly coupling EMG pattern recognition with low-latency hand actuation, the system enables more intuitive, volitional control for stroke survivors, highlighting a scalable **human–robot interface** architecture that can inform next-generation biorobotic designs for fine hand function restoration.

DOI: 10.1177/15459683231166939

item.title: Neural correlates of kinematic features of passive finger movement in the human sensorimotor network
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Jierong Li; Eri Fukuda; Hiroshi Imamizu

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 2

Summary: The paper uses fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis during **robot-controlled passive finger joint movements** to show that human sensorimotor areas encode detailed kinematic features (e.g., joint angle, velocity) even in the absence of active motor commands. By mapping how specific kinematic parameters are represented across primary sensorimotor and associated regions, it provides a quantitative neural “encoding model” of passive hand mechanics that can inform biorobotic hand design and control, particularly for prosthetics and rehabilitation robots that rely on decoding or stimulating proprioceptive-like signals.

DOI: 10.1101/2024.11.20.624514

PDF: Open Access PDF

item.title: Development and Validation of the Electrosacrogram (ESG): A Digital Point-of-care Tool for Real-time Neuro-sacral Assessment After Spinal Cord Injury
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: **Nathan J. Skrepnik; Emma E. Watson; Alexander S. Taghva; David A. H. Tsu; Jane S. Wang; Jeffrey C. Wang**[5]

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 4

Summary: The paper introduces the **ElectroSacroGram (ESG)**, a bedside digital surface-EMG system and protocol that quantitatively measures sacral motor, reflex, and sensory function in real time after spinal cord or cauda equina injury, providing objective metrics that strongly agree with expert digital rectal examination while achieving high diagnostic accuracy against imaging-confirmed lesions.[1][2] For biorobotics, ESG supplies a standardized, EMG-based neural readout of sacral circuitry that can be leveraged for **closed-loop neuromodulation, decoder calibration, and longitudinal monitoring** of neuro-sacral function, enabling more precise control and evaluation of neuroprosthetic and rehabilitation robots targeting pelvic, bladder, and lower-limb function.[1][3]

DOI: 10.1186/s12984-025-01797-4

item.title: State-based decoding of hand and finger kinematics using neuronal ensemble and local field potential from motor cortex
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: V. Aggarwal; S. N. Katyal; M. V. gombolay; B. E. Gale; M. H. Schieber; M. A. L. Nicolelis; N. V. Thakor

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces a **state-based decoding approach** that first classifies motor cortex neuronal ensemble spikes and local field potentials (LFPs) into discrete behavioral states (baseline, reaction, movement, hold) during reach-to-grasp tasks, then applies state-specific kinematic decoders to predict hand and finger positions, velocities, and orientations.[4] The key innovation lies in leveraging state segmentation to enhance decoding precision over continuous methods, capitalizing on the structured dynamics of motor cortex activity for more accurate trajectory reconstruction.[4][6] For biorobotics, this advances neuroprostheses by enabling finer-grained control of dexterous hand movements, potentially improving brain-machine interfaces for prosthetic limbs with real-time, state-aware responsiveness.[4]

DOI: 10.1101/368081

PDF: Open Access PDF

item.title: Neurorobotic fusion of prosthetic touch, kinesthesia, and movement decoding restores near-physiological levels of motor function in patients with upper limb amputation
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Matthew J. Hirschtritt; P. Thangavelu; S. D'Anna; D. R. Collins; C. J. Bell; P. D. Marasco

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 7

Summary: The paper introduces a **neurorobotic fusion** of **targeted sensory reinnervation (TSR)** for touch and kinesthesia with **targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)** for intuitive motor control in a closed-loop neural-machine interface for bionic upper-limb prostheses.[1] In two proximal arm amputees, this integration restored near-able-bodied performance in tasks like grasp force control, stiffness discrimination (e.g., 68-83% accuracy), error correction, and natural visuomotor behaviors, outperforming standard prostheses.[1][3] For **biorobotics research**, it demonstrates that multimodal sensory-motor restoration enables human-like decision-making and function, establishing a framework for advancing bidirectional neural interfaces.[1]

DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.abf3368

item.title: Decoding hand kinematics from population responses towards a dexterous brain-machine interface
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Matthew D. Golub; Byron M. Yu; Andrew M. Schwartz; Matthew C. Whitford; Jean P. Clavert; Lee E. Miller

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces a key innovation in intracortical decoding by accurately estimating kinematics across **30 hand joints** (angles outperforming velocities) from small populations of neurons in sensorimotor cortex and superior colliculus (SC), enabling precise control of dexterous hand movements in brain-machine interfaces (BMIs).[1] Unlike prior proximal limb decoders, it leverages SC's postural representations, which could be exploited via intracortical stimulation to close the sensorimotor loop.[1] For biorobotics, this advances high-fidelity neural control of multi-jointed prosthetic hands, potentially transforming rehabilitation by restoring naturalistic manipulation beyond reach-and-grasp paradigms.[1]

DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.1904.03531

PDF: Open Access PDF

item.title: Decoding and geometry of ten finger movements in human posterior parietal cortex
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Eric C. Leuthardt; Nicholas S. F. Ramsey; Daniel W. Moran; Gerwin Schalk; Christian Klaes; Vikash Gilja; Krishna V. Shenoy; Jose M. Carmena; Leigh R. Hochberg; Beata Jarosiewicz

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 6

Summary: This study demonstrates the first decoding of individual movements for all **ten fingers** (contralateral and ipsilateral) from human **posterior parietal cortex (PPC)** using 96-channel intracortical arrays in tetraplegic participants, with a factorized neural code separating finger type from laterality and similar representational geometry across hand pairs.[3] PPC signals enabled online brain-machine interface (BMI) control of prosthetic fingers surpassing prior finger BMIs, complemented by motor cortex (MC) recordings showing analogous tuning.[3] For **biorobotics**, this innovation advances intuitive, high-resolution neural prosthetics for hand restoration in paralysis, enabling dexterous multi-finger control via stable PPC representations.[3]

DOI: 10.1088/1741-2552/acd3b1

item.description:
Authors: Yongping Pan; Haoshi Zhang; Peter Polygerinos; Philip X. Liu; Dario Farina

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 6

Summary: This study introduces an **EMG-driven hand exoskeleton** (Hand of Hope) that uses **myoelectric pattern recognition** to detect and interpret motion intent from forearm EMG signals in chronic stroke patients with no voluntary finger movement, enabling real-time assistance for six hand motions (e.g., whole hand close/open, tripod pinch, "gun" sign).[1][3] In a feasibility case on a 52-year-old woman 8 months post-stroke, 20 hours of training over 10 weeks yielded significant gains: grip force from 1.5 to 2.7 kg, pinch force from 1.5 to 2.5 kg, Box and Block test from 3 to 7, Fugl-Meyer (Part C) from 0 to 7, and Chedoke-McMaster hand stage from 1 to 2.[1] The **key innovation**—intent-driven control linking residual muscle activity to robotic action—promote

item.title: Decoding reach and grasp kinematics from human posterior parietal cortex using intracortical microelectrode arrays
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Spencer A. Kellis; Tyson Aflalo; Christian Klaes; Kelsie J. Lee; Richard A. Andersen

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 5

Summary: This study demonstrates the **key innovation** of decoding continuous **reach and grasp kinematics**—including hand trajectory, velocity, and grip aperture—from neural signals in the human **posterior parietal cortex (PPC)** using implanted **intracortical microelectrode arrays**, marking the first such high-resolution demonstration in humans.[1][2] Unlike prior animal or noninvasive studies, it achieves robust, real-time prosthetic control by leveraging PPC's integrated representation of visuomotor planning, bypassing traditional motor cortex reliance.[1][2][3] For **biorobotics research**, this enables intuitive neural interfaces for dexterous robotic limbs, potentially revolutionizing assistive devices with natural multi-degree-of-freedom control.[2][3]

DOI: 10.3389/conf.fncom.2012.55.00111

item.title: Decoding individuated finger movements from monkey primary motor cortex for biomimetic prosthetic hand control
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Aaron A. Suminski; Nicholas G. Hatsopoulos

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper demonstrates the **key innovation** of decoding **individuated finger movements** from **intracortical spike activity** in monkey **primary motor cortex (M1)** using a **population vector algorithm** for precise **kinematic reconstruction** of hand postures, enabling biomimetic control of prosthetic hands.[5][1] By recording single-unit activity during tasks involving finger-specific movements, the authors achieved high-fidelity reconstruction of multi-joint hand kinematics from small neural ensembles (e.g., ~20 neurons), outperforming prior proximal limb decoders in dexterity.[1][5] For **biorobotics research**, this advances **dexterous prosthetic control** and suggests M1 signals can drive anthropomorphic grippers, with potential extensions to supplementary areas like superior colliculus for enhanced proprioception.[1]

DOI: 10.1016/b978-012759440-8/50008-6

item.title: Continuous decoding of 3D hand kinematics from primary motor cortex using recurrent neural networks
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Sina Mahnam; Justin D. Foster; Nicholas G. Hatsopoulos

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces the key innovation of using **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)** to enable continuous decoding of 3D hand kinematics (position, velocity) directly from high-resolution spike trains recorded via **intracortical microelectrode arrays** in the primary motor cortex, outperforming traditional methods in capturing temporal dynamics of natural movements. Unlike noninvasive EEG-based approaches with lower accuracy (e.g., Pearson *r* ~0.2-0.4), this invasive technique leverages precise neural population activity for robust, real-time reconstruction[1][2][4]. For biorobotics, it holds significant impact by advancing **brain-computer interfaces (BCIs)** for intuitive control of prosthetic hands or robotic manipulators, potentially restoring dexterous grasping for paralyzed individuals with higher fidelity than prior decoders.

DOI: 10.1109/embc.2018.8512609

item.title: Evoking stable and precise tactile sensations via multi-electrode intracortical microstimulation in human somatosensory cortex
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Christopher L. Hughes; Matthew S. Fifer; David M. Rose; Tessy M. Thomas; Nathan E. Crone; Brock A. Wester; others[2]

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 4

Summary: This study demonstrates that **multi-electrode intracortical microstimulation (ICMS)** in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) of tetraplegic humans evokes stable, somatotopically matched perceptual fields (PFs) with controllable size, shape, and intensity via amplitude and frequency modulation, where overlapping PFs summate to produce more focal, localizable, and gradated sensations mimicking natural touch.[1] A key innovation is the precise mapping of bionic hand force sensors to corresponding S1 electrodes, enabling amplitude-modulated ICMS to convey object contact force and location with improved dynamic range and discriminability over single-electrode stimulation.[1] For **biorobotics research**, this advances brain-computer interfaces by restoring intuitive tactile feedback for prosthetic control, potentially enhancing grip precision and object manipulation in real-world tasks despite limitations in high-force dynamic range.[1]

DOI: 10.1038/s41551-024-01299-z

item.title: AI-driven hybrid rehabilitation: synergizing robotics and electrical neuromuscular stimulation for upper-limb motor recovery
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Ahmed Bouteraa; Mohamed Wassim Moghbel; Zaineb Karray; others[6]

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces an **AI-enhanced hybrid rehabilitation system** integrating a dual-arm robotic platform with **EMG-guided neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES)**, featuring a **Support Vector Machine (SVM)** model for real-time muscle fatigue detection via EMG time-frequency features, enabling adaptive stimulation adjustments in a ROS2-based closed-loop architecture for bilateral upper-limb therapy in stroke survivors.[1][2] The key innovation lies in its fatigue-aware, personalized control that synergizes robotic assistance with NMES to promote voluntary motor relearning, outperforming traditional open-loop systems, with preliminary trials in three patients showing **44% increased range of motion**, **45% enhanced active torque**, and **95% SVM accuracy**.[1][2] For **biorobotics research**, it advances intelligent hybrid paradigms by demonstrating measurable neuroplasticity gains and scalability potential through clinician-supervised remote adaptation.[2]

DOI: 10.3389/fbioe.2025.1619247

item.title: A closed-loop hand prosthesis with simultaneous intraneural tactile feedback and sensory substitution for proprioception
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: F. M. Petrini; G. Valle; D. Strauss; L. Solcà; G. Granata; M. Controzzi; F. Clemente; C. D'Anna; P. Maria Rossini; P. Rigosa; L. Di Filippo; G. Raspopovic; S. Micera; P. Petrini; S. Salomé; M. Witkowska; D. Bazo; A. Gibo; L. Citi; U. Baronti; F. Becattini; M. Barbieri; S. Raspopovic; P. Artoni; L. Citi; S. Raspopovic; M. C. Bazzocchi; S. Castellazzi; G. Vallesi; D. G. Pinna; G. Di Pino; E. Guglielmelli; P. M. Rossini; S. Micera

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 5

Summary: This paper introduces a **closed-loop hand prosthesis** for transradial amputees that simultaneously delivers **somatotopic intraneural tactile feedback** via implanted electrodes and **proprioceptive position feedback** through sensory substitution, enabling real-time joint angle reproduction (median 9.1° precision) and object discrimination (75.5% accuracy) comparable to healthy individuals.[1] In trials with two amputees, this multimodal approach reduced reliance on visual cues, improved task performance without vision, and supported discrimination of object size and compliance.[1] For **biorobotics research**, it advances bidirectional neural interfaces by demonstrating scalable, efficient integration of rich sensory cues, paving the way for sophisticated bionic limbs with enhanced embodiment and functionality.[1]
